justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from the current price level, anchored by the assumption that the underlying asset continues along its recent trend with no major regime change. At the one-day horizon, I essentially anchored to the last known price, since within a single trading session the most likely outcome is mean-reversion to the prior close with minimal directional movement — hence both bounds of the confidence interval collapse to the point estimate itself, reflecting the near-certainty of opening near the prior close barring overnight news. At the one-week horizon, I projected a slight upward drift of roughly one percent, consistent with typical equity or commodity market behavior over short periods in a mild bull environment. At the one-month horizon, the drift compounds modestly further, though I recognize that a month is long enough for meaningful macro or fundamental developments to alter the trajectory.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty that characterizes random walk behavior in financial markets. At one week, a range of roughly 330 points on either side of the point estimate captures typical weekly volatility. By one month, that range widens to approximately 70 points on each side, reflecting the accumulation of daily shocks over roughly 20 trading days. The width is also influenced by the possibility of volatility clustering — if the market enters a high-volatility regime, realized outcomes could be much more dispersed than historical averages suggest.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic shocks such as an unexpected central bank decision, a geopolitical escalation, or a significant earnings surprise from a systemically important company. On the upside, stronger-than-expected economic data or a surprise policy easing could push prices well above my upper bounds. On the downside, a credit event, liquidity crisis, or sharp risk-off episode could breach the lower bounds. Black swan events, by definition, are not well-captured by historically calibrated intervals, so the tails of the true distribution are likely fatter than my stated 90% confidence intervals imply.

Finally, it is worth noting that my one-day interval is artificially tight because it was set equal to the point estimate, which assumes no overnight gap risk or pre-market information. In reality, even the one-day horizon carries meaningful gap risk from after-hours news, earnings releases, or geopolitical developments, meaning the true one-day uncertainty is somewhat wider than my forecast acknowledged.
